title: Ave Regina Caelorum

cards: Christmas gets packed away, and the song at the end of night prayer changes. The gate and the star step aside.
Then come the ashes, and Lent, and the song that stays through it sounds almost like a herald at a palace door: Ave, Regina caelorum. Hail, queen of heaven. Ave, Domina angelorum.
Hail, lady of the angels. Lent is purple cloth, fasting, the long walk toward the cross. Why greet a queen in a season like that?
The answer starts in a throne room, far back in the Bible.

teach.h: QUEEN BECAUSE HER SON IS KING.
teach.b: In the Book of Kings, King Solomon is on his throne when his mother, Bathsheba, comes in to speak to him. He stands, goes to meet her, bows to her, and has a throne set for her at his right hand.
Catholics call Mary queen for that kind of reason: not because she rules in her own right, but because her son is the king. Then the greetings. Ave, hail.
Salve, hail again. Gaude, rejoice. Vale, farewell.
The song is built almost entirely of greetings, like someone at a doorway who keeps finding another way to say hello. Then the root and the gate: salve, radix, salve, porta.
Hail, root; hail, gate; from you a light rose on the world. The root reaches back to Isaiah, in the Douay-Rheims: "there shall come forth a rod out of the root of Jesse." Jesse was David's father.
Christians read the new shoot from that old root as a promise of Christ, born into David's family, and see Mary as the one through whom he came.
The gate is the door the light came through, and in Lent, waiting for Easter light, the song keeps pointing at it.

teach.h: FAREWELL, AND PRAY TO CHRIST FOR US.
teach.b: Last, the farewell: vale, o valde decora, farewell, you who are so beautiful.

teach.h: THERE SHALL COME FORTH A ROD OUT OF THE ROOT OF JESSE.
teach.b: Then the final request: pray to Christ for us. A goodbye said before sleep, handing the singers on to her son. So a queen in Lent isn't so odd.
Lent walks toward the cross, and this song keeps a door open to the light on the other side.

how: Catholics who pray the Liturgy of the Hours traditionally close Night Prayer in Lent with the Ave Regina Caelorum, said or sung in Latin chant or in English.

o: Latin for a royal blessing before a meal
Latin for hail, queen of the heavens
Latin for the queen's palace in heaven

games.q: Ave Regina Caelorum — tap the pairs.

s: it closes night prayer in the season before Easter.
the song is all requests, with no greetings
it's built of greetings: ave, salve, gaude, vale.
Catholics call Mary queen because she rules in her own right
Catholics give another reason: her son is the king, as Bathsheba sat at Solomon's right hand.

games.q: you're King Solomon, on your throne. your mother, Bathsheba, walks in to speak to you. what do you do?
o: stay seated and hear her out.
rise, bow, and set a throne for her at your right hand.
send a servant to take her message.
games.why: in the Book of Kings he rises to meet her, bows, and has a throne set at his right hand. Catholics see Mary's queenship in that picture.

practice: Let today pass once, quickly, like a train watched from a platform, the morning, the middle, the evening, and then, the way the song does, say goodbye to it.
If you pray, close with the antiphon's first words, hail, queen of heaven, hail, lady of the angels, and its last request, pray to Christ for us. If you don't, end with one plain farewell to the day.

wordCard.voice: Ave Regina Caelorum. Hail, queen of the heavens: the night song of Lent, full of greetings, a root and a gate, and a goodbye before sleep.

orig.note: Latin: hail, queen of the heavens. caelorum is plural.
